about: The non-numeric claims of [JEngine], one record each: id, statement (in our vocabulary), source, kind, status, and either test (ASSERTED) or reason (PENDING / UNVERIFIABLE). See felizjueves.literature.claims. Ordered by id: add a record in its place rather than rewriting the file.

claims.statement: Alg. 1 line 10 writes J_p to global memory without atomics; once a class is split into batches, several kernels contribute to the same J_p, so the write needs atomics -- as §5 itself corrects.

Alg. 1 line 10 writes J[p] = 4 Jshm[p], and the factor 4 is never explained -- not in the algorithm, §3.3 or eqs. 19-22, where J_p = SUM_q [p|q] D_q carries no factor. It can only be a convention of the authors' pair lists or density (unique shell pairs, a doubled density), which the text does not state. This repo's kernel writes J_p unscaled and puts the only pair weight host-side (ao/j.py's unique sweep: ket off-diagonal weight 2, bra blocks scattered to both triangles; since milestone 7 the generated DQ kernel takes that weight as a host-supplied w and the JAB kernel scatters by the same rule), and J_mn then matches libcint's get_jk.

The best batch count per class depends on the GPU's memory system, not only on the class: on V100, A100 and GH200 the newer parts (larger L2) favour fewer batches -- L = 10 is best at 3 on A100 and GH200 and at 6 on V100, and [5|4] collapses on V100 (and less on A100) because its spills overflow L2 -- while above L = 12 the ranking agrees across all three despite their bandwidths, which the paper reads as high-L kernels being bound by memory latency rather than bandwidth; so the count should be chosen per hardware.
claims.reason: Timings of the authors' kernels on three NVIDIA data-centre GPUs (V100, A100, GH200), none of which this repo has; the latency reading rests on their Nsight Compute analysis. What is measured here is a different experiment on different hardware: data/measured/batch_recommendation.json (#56, recomputed by test/test_batchreport.py) gives each of OUR two cards its own best n_batches per (L, input), and it records where sm_86 and gfx1200 disagree. Whether batching moves our kernels across our ridge is #114's own claim, not this one.

claims.statement: A split class's batch count is a multiple of three, k sub-batches per direction, and the unsplit class is the one batch: partition refuses any count that is neither 1 nor a positive multiple of 3 (0, 2, 4, 5, a negative, and a non-int such as 3.0 or True). The paper's further claim that symmetry-breaking splits are worse is its own record, jengine/symmetry-breaking-splits-are-worse.

Under MILD (before the sieve), the only intermediates two batches of DIFFERENT directions share are the fundamentals (0,0,0)^(m), m > 0, and two sub-batches of the SAME direction share only axial intermediates (at most one non-zero component). Hence each batch kernel re-evaluates the Boys function for itself.

A target's batch direction is the axis of its largest component, a tie going to the cyclic predecessor: {x,y} -> x, {y,z} -> y, {x,z} -> z, and all three equal -> x. This is deliberately the opposite convention to MILD's.

THIS REPO'S claim, not the paper's: [JEngine, v2, §7.2]'s question -- does batching move a [p|q] kernel from memory-bound to compute-bound? -- asked of our generated kernels on our cards, under the rule issue #114 declared before any roofline row existed (felizjueves.ridge: for one arch and one L, batching crosses iff the cell is memory-bound at n_batches = 1 and compute-bound at some higher SUBGRID count; the per-kernel variant, every kernel of that count's partition compute-bound, scored separately). On sm_86 (RTX 3080, nvcc 13.0, ncu; measured ridge 0.65 FLOP/B) both variants give the same answers: at L = 16 batching CROSSES at 3 batches (the cell is memory-bound at 1 batch, 0.40 FLOP/B, and compute-bound at 3, 1.52 FLOP/B, every kernel of the 3-batch partition at 1.46 FLOP/B or more); at L = 7, 10 and 13 the cell is compute-bound ALREADY AT 1 BATCH (300, 3.54 and 0.96 FLOP/B), so batching does not cross -- there is nothing to cross, which is a statement about this card's low fp64 ridge; no L never crosses. On gfx1200 (measured ridge 1.49 FLOP/B) the answer is ABSENT: could not measure (measured_store.UNMEASURED, final since #140: rocprofv3 now loads, but gfx1200 defines no fp64 counter and its byte counters read 0 on this box), which is not 'never crossed'. Fig. 7's A100 ridge is a different number, and nothing here is compared with it.

Batching moves [p|q] kernels from memory-bound to compute-bound on the roofline: [5|5] is compute-bound from 3 batches and gains nothing beyond, [6|6] stays memory-bound at 1 and 3 and crosses at 6, and [7|7] needs at least 9 -- with some kernels of its 9-batch partition still memory-bound, so more batches might still help.
claims.reason: A roofline of the authors' kernels on an A100 (gly40/cc-pVQZ): its ridge is that card's fp64 peak over its bandwidth, and both the kernels and the card are out of reach here. #114 asked the same question of OUR kernels on sm_86 and gfx1200, under a rule declared in the issue before the roofline rows existed, and recorded the answer as this repo's own claim, jengine/batching-crosses-our-ridge (sm_86: crosses at 3 batches at L = 16 only, compute-bound already at 1 batch below it; gfx1200: could not measure); that answer is about our cards' ridge and does not discharge this one (the same split as jengine/nine-batches-suffice).

claims.statement: Raising the batch count lowers register use and spills, for two reasons together: fewer intermediates per batch, and fewer targets per batch, which narrows the J_p contraction each kernel carries.
claims.reason: The evidence is Table 4: spill and register counts of the authors' kernels through their compiler on an A100, deliberately not transcribed (data/literature/jengine/README.md says why). Our own spills on sm_86 and gfx1200 are measured (data/measured/kernels.json) and are a different claim; jengine/nine-batches-suffice's reason records one place where they do not fall with the batch count (gfx1200, 9 -> 12).

claims.statement: Raising the batch count lowers intermediates and targets per batch and raises total FLOPs across batches, because intermediates shared between batches are recomputed.
claims.reason: UNVERIFIABLE, decided by #116: no test can fail exactly when this claim is false. The claim is about the paper's post-sieve plans, and those depend on the sieve's seed order, which the paper does not publish and no rule recovers (#108, rules-only doctrine; limits.json). Worse, the paper's OWN printed Table 2 breaks the intermediates half at two steps (flat 95, 95 at L = 10 from 6 to 9 batches; rising 39 -> 40 at L = 7 from 6 to 9), so a test asserting the claim would fail on the source's own numbers, and a test pinning those exceptions holds our reconstruction, not the claim. What IS held, unmarked: the pre-sieve direction on our own counts (test/test_plan_dag.py::test_batching_trades_flops_for_intermediates: per-batch targets and intermediates do not rise and total FLOPs do not fall over 1 -> 3 -> 6 -> 9, L = 7..16), and the post-sieve exceptions below. The record of #12 and #108 follows. Post-sieve (#12) it holds at most cells but not at all of them. FLOPs are flat 1->3 at L = 7 (425, 425, where the paper prints 424, 425), and max intermediates per batch are flat 6->9 at L = 10 (95, 95). test/test_plan_sieve.py::test_batching_post_sieve pins both exceptions and carries no mark. #108's widened seed-order search (58 rules, plan/recovery.py seed_orders(widened=True), recovered cut) closes the L = 7 FLOP exception under 37 of them (424 -> 425, as printed) but moves no default, so the literal plan stays flat there; it does not close L = 10's flat intermediates, which are 95, 95 under all 58 orders and are 95, 95 in the paper's own Table 2. And the paper's Table 2 RISES at L = 7 from 6 to 9 batches (39 -> 40), which the recovered cut reproduces under all 58. So the source's own numbers contradict the intermediates half of the claim at two steps; test/test_plan_recovery.py::test_the_batching_exceptions_under_the_widened_family pins all three. No test can hold us to a direction the source's table does not keep.

claims.statement: The fastest batch count rises with L: no batching gain below L = 7, then 3 batches for most kernels at 8 <= L <= 10, 6 at 11-12 and 9 from 13 -- and the choice is largely independent of the molecule's size and composition (polyglycine, water, boron nitride), so a per-class table read off Fig. 8 serves as a general dispatch.
claims.reason: Kernel timings of the authors' kernels on an A100 inside EXESS, over molecules this repo does not run. The analogue measured here is a different experiment: data/measured/batch_recommendation.json (#56) derives a best n_batches per (L, card) from wall-clock on two synthetic inputs, and the two inputs (wide-T, near-T) do not always pick the same count, which is a dependence on the input that the paper's system-independence does not speak to. Dispatch is specification only in this repo (j_engine.md).

claims.statement: §8 says the batching strategy transitioned ALL high-angular-momentum kernels from memory-bound to compute-bound; §7.2 says some kernels of the 9-batch [7|7] partition remain memory-bound. The two sentences cannot both hold.
claims.reason: A contradiction between two sentences of the source about the authors' own A100 measurement; nothing in this repo depends on which one they meant. It is recorded because the distinction it blurs -- a class crossing the ridge versus every kernel of its partition crossing -- is exactly the cell-level versus per-kernel split #114 declares separately for our cards.

claims.statement: eq. 17 prints the unit vector 1y as (1,1,0); it is (0,1,0). (1,1,0) is not a unit vector and would break eq. 11.

At L = 6 the six batches are X_{0,2}, X_{3,6}, Y_{1,2}, Y_{3,6}, Z_{1,2}, Z_{3,6}: one cut (after a maximum component of 2) shared by all three directions, Y_{0,2} and Y_{1,2} (likewise Z) holding the same targets because no Y or Z target has a maximum component of 0.

The whole-J speedup from batching varies across molecules because of composition, not because batching a class becomes less effective: hydrogen-rich systems (water) spend less of their time in high-L classes than hydrogen-poor ones (boron nitride), and small systems lose some of the gain to kernel-launch overhead.
claims.reason: An explanation of the authors' whole-J timings in EXESS on an A100 over water clusters, polyglycine and boron nitride; this repo has neither the engine nor the systems at that size, and builds J_mn only at fixture size (through d on the cards), with every arithmetic step generated since milestone 7 but nothing of the new kernels timed and no whole-J timing across molecules of different composition.

claims.statement: The exchange matrix K_ab = SUM_cd D_cd (ac|bd) needs contraction work per primitive quartet that J does not: its output indices a and b straddle the bra pair record (a,c) and the ket pair record (b,d), so the ket's E transform (I[p] = SUM_q [p|q] E^bd_q), the bra's (V = SUM_p E^ac_p I[p]) and the D_cd digest all run inside the quartet loop. J pre-contracts its ket once per ket record (DQ: D_q) and back-transforms its bra once per bra class (JAB), so its [p|q] kernel does only J_p += SUM_q [p|q] D_q per quartet. Source: [JEngine, v2, §6], the sentence giving 'the additional contractions that must be completed at the shell quartet level' as K's reason.
claims.reason: No K kernel exists yet: milestone 10 declares this record before anything is built. The rule that will score it, fixed now: SHAPE, read off the kernel we build. The per-quartet body of a Target.K class (kernel_k.py, B2) inlines both E fragments (e_fragment.block_fragment for the (b,d) and the (a,c) pair records) inside the ket loop, while the Target.J [p|q] kernel at the same Spec.am inlines none. ASSERTED if that holds of the built IR for every K class built; refuted if K's per-quartet work can be written as J's (one pre-contracted ket vector per ket record, no E inside the quartet loop). Scored by E3.

claims.statement: Recomputing the fundamentals [r]^(0) in several kernels (a batched class, so that fewer kernels write the same output element) is worth more for K than for J, because what a split duplicates for K is the per-quartet E contraction (I and V into K[a,b]) and not only a reduction into J_p. A direction -- K's gain from splitting exceeds J's at the same L and batch count -- not a value. Source: [JEngine, v2, §6], the sentence that recomputing [r]^(0) 'has more merit when applied to the calculation of the exchange matrix K'.
claims.reason: Nothing to score yet: no K kernel and no K row. The rule that will score it, fixed now, before any row exists (#109's discipline): MONOTONICITY in two halves. Arithmetic (E1, fast tier): from the plan's batch partition and the E nonzero structure, count the work each extra batch duplicates, for J and for K at the same Spec.am and n_batches; K's duplicated contraction work must be strictly larger than J's. Measured (E2, both cards): the best-median wall-clock gain of the split K class over its same-session one-batch control must be at least the split J class's gain over its own, at the same L; contradicted on a card where J's gain is the larger. ASSERTED only if both halves hold on both cards; a card on which they disagree is recorded, never averaged. The verdict is open: Wang et al. profile high-l K as memory-bound. Scored by E3.

claims.statement: Splitting K's element-wise contributions across several kernels (the f-type K of Wang et al. [24], as the paper characterises it) has two effects together: each kernel uses fewer registers, and the kernels re-evaluate the same two-centre Hermite integrals redundantly. In our vocabulary: a split K class (one kernel per batch, B3) has, per batch kernel, no more registers and spill bytes than its one-batch K kernel, and its batch kernels together evaluate more Hermite intermediates than the one-batch kernel does. Source: [JEngine, v2, §1], the prior-art paragraph on Wang et al. [24].
claims.reason: No split K kernel exists yet (B3), and no K register row (E0, E2). The rule that will score it, fixed now: SHAPE, both effects required, on OUR split K kernels. (1) Every batch kernel's registers and spill bytes (sm_86: ptxas; gfx1200: kernel-resource-usage) are at or under the one-batch K kernel's at the same Spec.am, on both arches, and strictly under for at least one; (2) the summed count of Hermite intermediates evaluated across the batch kernels, counted from the built IR, is strictly greater than the one-batch kernel's. ASSERTED if both hold for every split K class measured; refuted at a class where either fails. It characterises another group's kernels, so a refutation says our split does not show the effect, not that theirs did not. Scored by E3.

claims.statement: The per-record product key I_q * max_q |D_q| is the better ket sort key than one global max|D| (ket key I_q * Dmax_global, the order by I_q alone -- the density_sort=False fallback jgen kept and never measured): at the same tau, molecule and batch count it screens more (bra, ket) record pairs and so builds J_p faster. The measured arm of jengine/ket-sort-key-is-the-product.
claims.reason: A statement about the paper's kernel on its A100, which nothing here runs. What #147 measured instead, on OUR cards, under a rule declared in the issue ("Expectation: the global key is worse. If it is not, that is the result") and transcribed into felizjueves.measured_store's docstring (THE SORT KEY) before any of its rows existed -- per cell the global key is WORSE iff its build's median is slower than the product's by more than the larger IQR (#60's rule), BETTER iff faster by that, else UNRESOLVED; WORSE on an arch iff at every cell; CONTRADICTED iff BETTER at any -- is that the verdict is CONTRADICTED on BOTH cards. The cells: H2O/cc-pVDZ (dispatched, 25 classes) and a two-H2 chain (one class) at tau = 1e-3 and 1e-10, both arms of each in one gated session per card (data/measured/builds.json, arm 'sort-ab'). The SCREEN goes the expected way everywhere: the global key skips NO pair on any cell (the product skips 123896 and 15684 of 351649 on H2O/cc-pVDZ, 2790 and 560 of 8100 on the chain; and 66060 and 36072 of 104976 on #88's four-H2 chain, oracle only), because I_pair is pair-factor-free and a ket's distance decay lives in its Dmax alone, which a global value erases. The CLOCK does not: the global key is WORSE only on the chain at tau = 1e-3 (sm_86 285.7 against 255.4 us; gfx1200 251.5 against 211.6 us), and BETTER on the chain at tau = 1e-10 (sm_86 285.7 against 346.7 us; gfx1200 251.0 against 273.8 us) and on H2O/cc-pVDZ at 1e-10 on gfx1200 (7.06 against 8.75 ms) and at 1e-3 on sm_86 (8.51 against 10.08 ms, by 1.57 ms over a 1.36 ms IQR, on a card whose cc-pVDZ timings are bimodal near 8.5 and 10 ms); the remaining two cells are UNRESOLVED (data/literature/jengine/limits.json). Where the product key skips little, its ORDER costs more time than its skips save -- the global arm differs from it in ket order and keys only. Held, cell by cell, by measure/measure_store.py::test_the_sort_key_verdict_is_contradicted_on_both_cards.

claims.statement: Kets are sorted descending by the per-record product I_q * max_q |D_q| (the pair-factor-free Schwarz bound times the largest weighted, dressed density element of that ket record), and that order is what makes the screen's break sound: with a fixed I_bra >= 0, I_bra * key is non-increasing along the list, so the first ket under tau ends the row with nothing lost. Under another key the same break is unsound -- ordered by I_q alone (the order of jgen's global-max|D| fallback) or left in pair order, it drops kets that clear tau, and J leaves the screen's own error bound tau * scale. The global-max|D| key used as the screen's key too is sound but looser (it skips no more). This record is the structural half; whether the product is the better key in time on a card is the measured arm, jengine/ket-sort-key-beats-the-global-max (#147), which the rows of this box's two cards contradict.

eq. 13 prints the fundamental's m-dependence as (-2 theta)^m; it is (-2 theta^2)^m (McMurchie-Davidson's (-2 alpha)^j with alpha = theta^2). Only the latter makes d/dPQ_x [0]^(m) = PQ_x [0]^(m+1), which eqs. 10-12 assume, so (-2 theta)^m is wrong in every class that reaches m > 0 (every class above (ss|ss)) whenever theta != 1. reference.pq forms (-2 theta^2)^m, and ERI blocks built from it match libcint's int2e class by class; with the base perturbed -- the printed -2 theta, or -2 theta^2 scaled by 1 + 1e-9 -- every fast-tier class above (ss|ss) fails that comparison and (ss|ss), which reaches only m = 0, is bit-for-bit unchanged (#120).

At one batch, kernels go from compute-bound at low L (L <= 6, whose intermediates fit on chip) to progressively memory-bound as L rises, because the intermediates spill out of registers; moving a kernel back to compute-bound can be worth up to an order of magnitude.
claims.reason: A roofline of the authors' kernels on an A100 (gly20/cc-pVQZ), and the L <= 6 boundary is that card's. Our own one-batch kernels over the subgrid's L have roofline rows on sm_86 only (#112, data/measured/roofline.json; gfx1200 could not measure, measured_store.UNMEASURED), which is a different experiment: our cards' measured fp64 ridges (0.65 and 1.49 FLOP/B, data/measured/ceilings.json) are far below an A100's, so the boundary need not fall anywhere near L = 6. On sm_86 it falls between L = 13 and 16: one batch is compute-bound at L = 7, 10 and 13 (300, 3.54 and 0.96 FLOP/B) and memory-bound at L = 16 (0.40), the direction the claim states but at that card's boundary, with four L sampled (felizjueves.ridge; test/test_ridge.py recomputes it).

claims.statement: The MILD tree obeys Johnson, Gill & Pople's optimal-tree rules 1, 2, 3 and 5: axial integrals {0 0 j} always present; reduce the unit component of {0 1 j}; never reduce the j of {1 1 j}; reduce the 2 of {0 2 j}.

The MILD tree alone (before the sieve) is optimal in intermediates below L = 5 and not from L = 5 on. Held where plan/optimum.py (#106) is exact, L <= 5: MILD's one-batch point equals the exact frontier for L <= 4, and at L = 5 it is (51 intermediates, 161 FLOPs) against the frontier's single point (48, 160), strictly dominated (#111's measurement, data/literature/jengine/mild_vs_optimum.json). L >= 6 is beyond the exact search; a beam there bounds the gap from below only.

MILD reduces along the smallest non-zero component of r (zeros excluded from the minimum) and breaks a tie toward the cyclic successor: rx=ry<rz -> y, ry=rz<rx -> z, rx=rz<ry -> x, and all three equal -> z.
Against Johnson et al.'s near-optimal tree search, MILD costs 1-2% more FLOPs and has 2-6% fewer intermediates.
claims.reason: A comparison against a search that is not here: Johnson et al.'s near-optimal tree search (the paper's refs 59/60), whose code, output, grid, cost convention and reference point are all unavailable (data/literature/jengine/limits.json records it as not reproducible on this machine). #111 REPLACED the comparison rather than re-running it: data/literature/jengine/mild_vs_optimum.json measures MILD (no sieve) against this tree's own exact optimum (plan/optimum.py, one reduction direction per materialised node, L <= 5), and DISAGREES with the printed percentages -- equal through L = 4, and at L = 5 behind on BOTH axes, +6.25% intermediates and +0.625% FLOPs, where the paper says 2-6% ahead and 1-2% behind; every exact frontier is a single point, so nothing in the space is ahead of it on either axis. #111 first marked this record asserted on the test that pins that gap; #116 demoted it, because that test fails if the paper's percentages held here and passes when they are false, which is the opposite of a witness. The test now holds jengine/mild-suboptimal-from-l5, the half of §4.1 this tree can compute.

claims.statement: For L <= 16, at most 9 batches are needed; the batch counts worth generating over are 1, 3, 6 and 9.
claims.reason: The claim is relative to the paper's register and shared-memory budget on their A100, which no measurement here reaches. What #60 measured instead, on OUR cards and under a definition declared before the 12-batch rows existed (felizjueves.measured_store's docstring, NINE AGAINST TWELVE: 9 suffices at (arch, L) iff the 12-batch cell neither has fewer summed spills nor is faster, on the wide-T or near-T input, by more than the larger IQR; on an arch iff at every L in {7, 10, 13, 16}), is that 9 does NOT suffice on either card. sm_86 (nvcc 13.0): b 12 spills less at L 13 (14472 -> 12048 bytes) and L 16 (181224 -> 146020), though it is slower than b 9 at every L on both inputs. gfx1200 (hipcc / ROCm 7.2.4): b 12 spills more at every spilling L and is slower on wide-T everywhere, but is faster on near-T at L 16 (303.5 -> 299.4 ms, beyond the 0.8 ms IQR). #93 re-timed every subgrid cell behind the card-utilisation gate, one session per card, and the verdict is unchanged cell for cell; the medians quoted here are #93's. Held, cell by cell, by measure/measure_store.py::test_nine_batches_do_not_suffice_on_either_card; data/measured/kernels.json has the rows.

claims.statement: Choosing an optimal batching is an NP-hard partitioning problem, and its cost function needs the MD search tree re-solved for every candidate batch, which is why both the tree and the batching are solved heuristically.
claims.reason: A complexity claim, stated without a proof or a reduction and without a citation; no finite computation establishes NP-hardness. What this repo can say is narrower: plan/search.py searches the cut space the paper's scheme admits, and plan/optimum.py's exact tree search stops at L = 5 on cost (its CEILING_REASON), which is consistent with the claim and does not prove it.

claims.statement: eq. 13's fundamental keeps (2/sqrt(pi)) theta and not the pair factors. McMurchie-Davidson's ERI prefactor lambda = 2 pi^{5/2} / (zeta eta sqrt(zeta+eta)) factors exactly as (2/sqrt(pi)) theta * (pi/zeta)^{3/2} * (pi/eta)^{3/2}, theta^2 = zeta*eta/(zeta+eta), so the pair factors go with the E coefficients -- (pi/zeta)^{3/2} on the bra pair, (pi/eta)^{3/2} on the ket pair, both by ao.pairs.dress, the one dressing function -- and the three placements multiply back to lambda: none missing, none applied twice. Witnessed per angular-momentum class against libcint's int2e (#85's blocks; s/p fast, d and above slow), with no class boundary (#121): all 55 canonical classes of HF/cc-pVTZ, s to f, L = 0..12 -- L <= 8 in test/oracle/fixtures/hf_ccpvtz_eri.json, L = 9..12 one file each in hf_ccpvtz_eri_l9..l12.json, every file under the 512 KB hook -- plus H2O/6-31G's six s/p classes (h2o_631g_eri.json): dress scaled by 1 + 1e-9, or (pi/zeta)^1 in place of ^{3/2}, fails every fast-tier class. The comparison sees the PRODUCT: a constant moved between dress and the fundamental (dress * 2 with 2/sqrt(pi) / 4) passes every block (and J), and what fails then is the in-repo absolute pins of each half: the fundamental by test/test_theta_convention.py's [0]^(0) = erf(theta R)/R and test_reference_pq.py's defining integral, the dressing by test_ao_pairs.py's dressed-overlap checks (the dressed t = 0 column is the overlap; a unit self-overlap) -- so with those, the placement, not only the product, is held (#90; j_engine.md, 'The Coulomb matrix, witnessed from outside').

MILD cannot obey rule 4 (reduce to a parent and grandparent already in the tree): that is a property of the graph built so far, while MILD is a pure function of r. The sieve is the pass that recovers it.
The sieve's effect on register spills is non-monotone across classes: about 4% fewer on average, but [5|6] gets 3% more and [8|8] 11% fewer.
claims.reason: A spill count is a measurement of the paper's kernels on their compiler and their card (an A100), not a property of the tree -- the same argument that keeps Table 4 out of data/ -- and our sieve is a reconstruction whose seed order is not recovered (#108). What #164 read instead, on #162's rows (the 20 subgrid cells and L = 11, one batch, each no-sieve arm against its sieved control, per card), by the two questions the issue asked before those rows existed -- does the mean fall, and is the effect non-monotone across classes -- read as felizjueves.measured_store.sieve_spills states (the per-class mean of (sieved - unsieved) / unsieved over the cells that spill; non-monotone iff more spills at some cell and fewer at another; [8|8] at L = 16, one batch; [5|6] at (6,0|5,0), i.e. [6|5], the only L = 11 kernel recorded): the NON-MONOTONICITY reproduces on both cards, and [8|8] spills less with the sieve on both ([8|8] -3.78% and -2.50% on sm_86 and gfx1200, not 11%). The rest does not: the [5|6] stand-in spills LESS on both ((6,0|5,0) -7.25% and -0.63%, not 3% more), and the per-class mean falls on one card only (sm_86 +1.45%, gfx1200 -0.24%; the summed spills -0.97% and -0.34%). So the published pattern fails on both cards, and a test asserting it would fail on our rows without making the paper's claim false, so it cannot be the claim's witness (#116's argument). On gfx1200 a spill is hipcc's spilled-register count, not bytes. data/literature/jengine/limits.json records the mechanism; held, half by half and cell by cell, by measure/measure_sieve_spill_claim.py::test_the_sieve_spill_pattern_on_both_cards.

claims.statement: Alg. 3 leaves three choices open: the order targets are seeded into the queue (line 4) -- §4.1 says the result depends on it, by up to ~2%, and does not give the order; which other direction a child is re-expanded in (line 12); and how far 'any unnecessary parents of i' reaches when i is deleted (line 16).
claims.reason: An omission in the source: no test can recover what the text does not carry. #160 names all three choices, and what this repo does for each, in one file: data/literature/jengine/seed_order_spread.json's open_choices. Lines 12 and 16 are fixed by our own choice (plan/sieve.py's docstring; docs/implementation/mild.md), each a StructuralLimit in limits.json ('sieve re-expansion direction', 'sieve deletion reach') and each pinned by tests in test/test_plan_sieve.py so the choice cannot move silently; those tests hold our reconstruction, not the paper's unstated choice. For line 4, #108 searched a family of seed-order RULES (plan/recovery.py, seed_orders(widened=True)) and none reproduces every Tables 1-2 cell, so under the rules-only doctrine the order is recorded as not recovered (limits.json). The quantitative half, '~2%', stays unverifiable too, for a reason #172's wider search sharpens rather than removes: it is a range over the paper's own seed orders, which the paper does not state, and neither of this repo's two spaces is that one. Over the 58 rules the spread is up to 3.706% on FLOPs and 2.946% on max intermediates (seed_order_spread.json, recomputed by test/test_plan_recovery.py; limits.json's 'seed-order spread'). Over #172's per-batch permutations climbed from those rules (data/scoreboards/jengine/searched_cuts.json) there is no range to read: the climb is a minimisation that records only its frontier, so it bounds a cell's low end and never its high end. What that space does show is that the order moves the result further than the rules do. At all 6 cells where the printed FLOPs lie below every one of the 58 rules, a climbed order is at or under them, and the searched plans are at or under the printed value in all three tables in all 40 cells (22 exactly, 18 under). So some seed order reaches every printed cell. That is consistent with 'the result depends on the order' and says nothing about how far the paper's orders range. Held by test/test_claims.py::test_the_sieve_claim_reads_the_searched_space (these figures, against searched_cuts.json and seed_order_spread.json) and test/test_plan_recovery.py::test_the_sieve_claim_and_mild_md_quote_the_spread (the status and the 58-rule figures).

claims.statement: Splits that break the three-way symmetry (a batch count other than 1 or a multiple of three) are both unnecessary and worse than the symmetric ones. Measured on OUR cards (#113) by a study path that builds the asymmetric batch list itself (felizjueves.asym; Spec and partition still refuse it): L in {13, 16} x n_batches in {4, 5, 7, 8}, each split minimax by the paper's own criterion, timed against its two nearest legal counts in the same session on both of #53's inputs. Under the rule declared before any asymmetric row existed, every cell is slower than its best legal neighbour on at least one input and faster on none, on sm_86 and on gfx1200 (spills and registers reported, not judged).

theta appears in eq. 13 (the fundamental) and is never defined; the conventional McMurchie-Davidson reading is theta^2 = zeta*eta/(zeta+eta), and that theta and no other is what the generated kernel's prelude forms (as do reference.pq and ao/). Witnessed from OUTSIDE (#90): J_mn with every J_p from the interpreted generated kernel (ao.drive.KernelJP through ao.j's jp= seam) matches PySCF/libcint's get_jk fixture to the derived 1e-12 scale_J. Perturbing theta consistently at every site that forms it (the kernel prelude, ao/j.py, ao/eri.py), so that the internal reference/pq comparison still agrees to 0, moves H2/STO-3G to 8.85e-10 scale_J at a relative theta error of 1e-9, and to 0.35-0.50 scale_J under the slip readings (theta^2 unrooted, sqrt(zeta+eta), sqrt(zeta*eta)). The fast-tier H2 cases reach theta through F_0 only; the slow H2O cases (to cc-pVDZ, l <= 2) reach it through m > 0 too. test/test_theta_convention.py stays the in-repo closed-form anchor (erf(theta R)/R) and the emitted-text check, unmarked.
